title: A Cost-Optimized 5-Protein Panel for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Diagnosis
author: Wenhua Lv
materials: Predict probabilities on the test set. (
Compare ProtRS with PRS and clinical risk factors
Extract the standard PRS for SLE.

steps.title: Extract case and control cohorts
steps.instruction: Obtain UK Biobank approved data, extract 48,036 control individuals from the non‑cancer self‑reported population without SLE or related autoimmune conditions, and extract SLE cases using ICD‑9/ICD‑10 codes and self‑report while excluding other autoimmune diseases.

steps.title: Impute and standardize protein data
steps.instruction: For each of the 2,923 plasma proteins, replace missing values (NA) with the protein’s mean across all samples, then center and scale each protein to zero mean and unit variance.

steps.title: Identify SLE‑associated proteins (LASSO BCCS)
steps.instruction: Run 1,000 balanced case‑control subsampling (BCCS) iterations of LASSO logistic regression to select stable proteins.

substeps.instruction: Set random seed for reproducibility (e.g., set.seed(123)).
For iteration = 1 to 1,000:
1. Randomly sample from the control pool a number of controls equal to the number of SLE cases (n = 544) to create a 1:1 balanced case‑control set.
2. Fit LASSO logistic regression (glmnet, family = "binomial", alpha = 1) with disease status as outcome and all 2,923 proteins as predictors.
3. Select the penalty parameter λ by 10‑fold cross‑validation using lambda.min (minimum mean cross‑validated error).
4. Record the non‑zero coefficients and corresponding protein names.
After completing 1,000 iterations, count the selection frequency for each protein (how many iterations it had a non‑zero coefficient).
Retain proteins selected in ≥500 iterations (≥50 % frequency) as stable SLE‑associated biomarkers.
For each retained protein, compute its final coefficient as the median of its non‑zero coefficients across all iterations where it was selected.

steps.title: Compute Protein Risk Score (ProtRS)
steps.instruction: For each individual j, calculate ProtRS = Σ (β_i × Prot_ij), where β_i is the final median coefficient from the previous step and Prot_ij is the centered‑and‑scaled level of protein i for individual j.

steps.title: Evaluate 35‑protein model (BCCS)
steps.instruction: Assess the predictive performance of the full 35‑protein ProtRS model using 1,000 BCCS iterations.

substeps.instruction: For each of 1,000 BCCS iterations (new random control subset):
1. Split the balanced set into training (70 %) and testing (30 %).
2. Fit a logistic regression model: SLE ~ ProtRS + age + gender on the training set.
3. Predict probabilities on the test set.
4. Calculate AUC, accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, and F1 using the pROC and caret packages.
Aggregate the 1,000 metric values and report the median and the 95 % uncertainty interval (2.5th and 97.5th percentiles).

steps.title: Evaluate alternative risk models
steps.instruction: Using the same 1,000 BCCS iterations, build and compare additional logistic models.

substeps.instruction: Model PRS: SLE ~ PRS + age + gender.
Model clinical: SLE ~ smoking + sleep_duration + insomnia + PM2.5 + age + gender.
Categorise continuous variables as described: PM2.5, PRS, and ProtRS by quartiles; sleep duration into a 9‑hour category.
Evaluate performance metrics (AUC, accuracy, etc.) as in the previous step and compare results with bar plots.

steps.title: Rank proteins and test reduced panels
steps.instruction: Determine how model performance changes when using fewer top‑ranked proteins.

substeps.instruction: Rank the 35 stable proteins by descending selection frequency (from Step 3).
For k = 1 to 35:
1. Take the top k proteins.
2. Compute ProtRS_k as the weighted sum using their median coefficients.
3. Repeat the 1,000 BCCS evaluation (training/testing logistic regression with ProtRS_k) as in Step 5.
Plot performance metrics (AUC, accuracy, etc.) against the number of proteins k.

steps.title: Identify cost‑effective optimum
steps.instruction: Select the smallest protein set that yields minimal loss of performance: the top 5 proteins (TRIM21, SOD2, KLK3, IL15, ADIPOQ) achieve AUC = 0.82 while reducing assay costs by approximately 87 % compared with the 35‑protein panel.

steps.title: Compute population attributable fractions
steps.instruction: Estimate PAF for each risk factor using discrete categories and the graphPAF package.

substeps.instruction: Discretise variables as in previous steps: ProtRS, PRS, and PM2.5 by quartiles; insomnia, smoking as binary; sleep duration as described.
Use graphPAF::PAF_calc_discrete() with PAF = 1 – Σ(p_i / RR_i), where p_i is the proportion in exposure level i and RR_i is the relative risk from logistic regression.
Repeat the calculation for each of the 1,000 BCCS iterations and report the median PAF with 95 % uncertainty interval.

steps.title: Test alternative imputation methods
steps.instruction: Assess robustness of ProtRS and model performance to different missing‑value strategies.

substeps.instruction: Replace mean imputation (Step 2) with one of: multiple imputation by chained equations (mice), median imputation, or k‑nearest neighbours (k = 5, VIM::kNN).
Re‑compute ProtRS and repeat model performance evaluation (AUC).
Verify that Pearson correlation between the new ProtRS and the original mean‑imputed ProtRS exceeds 0.96.

steps.title: Increase iteration stability
steps.instruction: Repeat the LASSO BCCS procedure with more iterations to test stability of selected proteins.

substeps.instruction: Run Step 3 with 10,000 BCCS iterations for LASSO, retaining proteins selected in ≥50 % of iterations.
Compare the resulting protein set with the original 1,000‑iteration set using a Venn diagram (Figure S5); expect >97 % concordance.
